title: Claude Enterprise Automation: A Complete 2026 Guide
summary: Claude enterprise automation runs scheduled work within admin-set limits. You'll understand the cost structure and configuration process for deployment.
body_markdown:
## Where Activepieces fits around Claude Enterprise


Activepieces doesn't fix what admin visibility can't show you.


It's a separate workflow tool with 747 integrations in its open source repo that sits outside your Claude Enterprise controls and calls Claude through the Anthropic API as a single step, and it doesn't configure seats, SSO or connectors, so any employee could invoke any of the 747 integrations without your enterprise oversight.


### When a separate workflow tool is worth it


Use one when the job spans several business apps and needs triggers, approval gates and retries. A request arrives, a person approves it, a record updates in your CRM, and a failed call gets retried without anyone re-running it by hand.


Forcing that orchestration into Claude Enterprise, which isn't built for it, means someone pastes outputs between systems manually, which is where unreviewed changes slip through.


If your policy requires workflow logic and run history to stay inside your own infrastructure, Activepieces can also be self-hosted, and that option matters: the free Community Edition is the MIT-licensed core running on your own servers.


It also means you now own another system with its own access list, and you have to administer it like one.


Triggers and approval boxes feed an Activepieces flow, and flows are unlimited on every plan including free, that holds one Anthropic API step and then a business app, while a separate Claude Enterprise box holds seats, SSO and connectors.


The flow runs on API credentials, and the Enterprise box governs people.


### How the processing step functions?


Inside the flow, the Claude step is a single action: it sends a prompt and the incoming data to the Anthropic API and passes the response to the next step. It doesn't approve anything, and it doesn't decide who may trigger the flow.


That has a practical consequence. Your SSO rules and seat assignments in Claude Enterprise don't apply to this step, because it authenticates with an API key.


Whoever can edit the flow can change the prompt and reach the key's spend.


Activepieces closes that gap by putting the agent inside the same access model as your staff: RBAC, SSO and SCIM decide who may edit a flow and which connections an agent may use, and the Ultimate tier adds custom roles and audit logs.


The run detail view for an agent step lists each tool call on its own line, with its own input and output instead of one merged result, and the enterprise RBAC documentation applies those same access policies to what an agent may connect to.


MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run it in production.


Put the approval box before any step that writes to a business app, restrict flow editing to named people, and keep the key's access narrow. The next section covers how to set those limits.
